statements.text: Maybe our competitive advantage today will not be the same just a few short years from now, given the pace, the rate of change that we're observing in AI space.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI and IP, Part I: Patents, Innovation, and Competition.

statements.text: everybody's talking about all the bad things that could happen with AI, ``I, Robot,'' the zombie apocalypse, and the good things that are going to happen category. [...] even if we chose not to participate as a nation, it's going to happen. So the question is whether or not the United States is going to maintain a leadership position in innovation and what I think is one of the most promising spaces for future innovation that we have today.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary IP Subcommittee hearing on AI and intellectual property, featuring Senator Tillis's opening remarks before witness testimony.

statements.text: And one of the subjects that we're talking about are the possible results from improperly developed and secured models. [...] all of them are safe.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property.

statements.text: I am not in that camp. I think that AI is good. [...] It is a matter of getting the regulatory construct, the intellectual property construct, all the other underlying policies that you need when a new, I think positive—in a positive term, disruptive technology hits the field.
statements.context: Senate IP Subcommittee hearing on AI and copyright law, Part II, chaired by Senator Coons.

statements.text: First, it is critical to include IP considerations in any regulatory framework for artificial intelligence and to give our Copyright Office, in this framework, a seat at the table. [...] We should also consider whether changes to our copyright laws or whole new protections like a Federal right of publicity may be necessary to strike the right balance between creators' rights and AI's ability to enhance innovation and creativity.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on AI and copyright, Part II.

statements.text: a recent survey on how consumers view AI found that most consumers, nearly 80 percent, believe the use of AI should be explicitly disclosed.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee hearing on Artificial Intelligence and Intellectual Property—Part II: Copyright.

statements.text: So, that entire musical rendition is a product of AI. [...] that image—one of those, that name, image, and likeness, is something that is the property of Tupac's estate.
statements.context: Senate hearing on the No Fakes Act, a bill to protect individuals from unauthorized AI-generated digital replicas of their name, image, and likeness.

statements.text: one of the reasons you maybe got emotional is because this is an existential threat to creators. And I'm trying to figure out how we educate people on the difference between an original creation from a human being and something that was either created or augmented from a machine.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the No Fakes Act, during Senator Tillis's questioning round.

statements.text: We don't even know what AI is going to look like, 10 years from now.
statements.context: Senate Judiciary Subcommittee on Intellectual Property hearing on the NO FAKES Act, which addresses unauthorized digital replicas and deepfakes.

statements.text: It reinforces what we've heard today, why we need a clear policy to protect image, voice, and likeness of all individuals from unauthorized AI replicas.
statements.context: Closing remarks at a Senate Judiciary Committee hearing on the No Fakes Act, which protects individuals from unauthorized AI-generated digital replicas of their image, voice, and likeness.
